bull_bear.body:
- Quality and food-safety accreditation at the producing estate (ISO 9001:2015, ISO 22000:2018, HACCP by KVQA) plus Trustea sustainable-tea verification by Control Union.
- Realisation-led rather than volume-led: 'Our average realization has gone up by 7.00% in comparison to the previous year resulting in improved financial performance of the division.'
- Orthodox capability upgraded during the year with new rolling tables, balance shifters, sorting machines, colour sorter, dryer and ATM heater, which management says will save cost and improve quality.
- Stable controlling shareholder: Rydak Enterprises & Investment Limited holds 50,60,870 equity shares, i.e. 56.19% of share capital.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Climate change and shifting weather patterns — The MD&A names climate change as reducing both tea yield and quality, and says changes in weather pattern affect the timing of the tea flushes, making production less predictable - a direct hit to a single-crop plantation.
- Cost inflation across the plantation cost base — The MD&A lists rising cost of wages, fertilizers, chemicals, power and fuel, transportation and packaging as a main challenge; with wages set under plantation labour law this is largely non-discretionary.
- Labour availability and plantation labour regulation — Labour shortages are named as an industry challenge; the Company runs a labour-intensive estate with 1477 permanent employees as on 31.03.2026 and is tested for compliance with the Assam Tea Plantation Labour Act, 1951.
- Import competition — Import competition is listed among the main challenges faced by the Indian tea industry, capping domestic price realisation.
- Single-commodity, single-division concentration — The secretarial auditor records that 'The Company is engaged in the business of tea' and the notes carry the Textile business only as 'Since Discontinued', so earnings depend entirely on one crop at the Tea Division, whose only named unit is the Ananda Tea Estate.
- Volume volatility versus price-led earnings — Black Tea production moved down by about 14% in FY2025-26 while the result was carried by a 7.00% rise in average realisation; the North Eastern India average price itself rose about 11.23% off an unusually strong auction year, so a price reversal would not be cushioned by volume.

business.body: The Company is engaged in the business of tea: it grows and manufactures Black Tea, including orthodox grades, through its Tea Division, whose named operating unit in this report is the Ananda Tea Estate. The industry-specific laws the secretarial auditor tests it against - the Tea Act, 1953, the Assam Tea Plantation Labour Act, 1951 and the Food Safety Standard Act, 2006 - describe a labour-intensive plantation operation, with 1477 permanent employees on the rolls as on 31.03.2026. The Textile business is carried in the notes only as 'Textile (Since Discontinued)', so tea is the continuing operation.

outlook.body:
- Outlook for FY2026-27 is described as 'cautiously optimistic': volume growth is likely to remain steady but value growth will be driven by premium products, wellness positioning and ready-to-drink formats.
- Management expects focus on branding, speciality teas and sustainability to outperform.
- Rising disposable incomes and a growing middle-class population are said to be fuelling demand for high-end and health-related tea.
- FY2025-26 was a positive year for the Indian tea industry - record export, strong prices and healthy domestic consumption outweighed production, with robust export demand particularly for orthodox tea.
- Pricing backdrop: the overall North Eastern India average was 224.00 in FY2025-26 against 201.39 in FY2024-25, an overall increase of about 11.23%.
- Company-level mix effect: Black Tea production moved down by about 14% versus the previous year while average realisation rose 7.00%.
- Structural supports cited: Tea Board of India plans and developments, ATISIS/TRUSTEA programmes for specialty and orthodox tea, technological modernisation of manufacturing, climate-resilient cultivation and advances in new and innovative packing materials.
- Cost and supply headwinds cited: climate change reducing tea yield and quality, shifting weather patterns making flush timing and production less predictable, rising cost of wages, fertilizers, chemicals, power and fuel, transportation and packaging, labour shortages and import competition.
